# Smart Charger Voltage Behavior and Battery Safety

A reading of 15.7V on a smart charger for 12V lead-acid batteries is actually standard behavior during the absorption phase, not a malfunction. The device is functioning as designed by pushing current into the battery bank until the terminal voltage hits the preset float or absorption target. If your unit is rated for 2A, 4A, or 6A, it will automatically regulate that current output while maintaining the required voltage profile to complete the charge cycle safely.

The confusion often stems from a misunderstanding of how constant-current (CC) and constant-voltage (CV) charging profiles interact. When you connect a battery with low internal resistanceâlike a healthy flooded lead-acid or AGM unitâthe charger attempts to raise the voltage to its maximum setting for the selected ampere rating. For a 6A charger targeting a 12V system, hitting 15.7V indicates the battery has reached approximately 80% to 90% state of charge. At this point, the charger switches from constant current mode to constant voltage mode. It holds the voltage steady at roughly 14.4V for AGM or 13.5Vâ14.2V for flooded types, depending on temperature compensation settings, while the amperage tapers down naturally.

If you see a sustained reading of 15.7V and the current is not tapering off, two scenarios are likely: either the battery is severely sulfated with high internal resistance preventing voltage rise, or the charger's logic board has failed to switch modes. A healthy 12V lead-acid battery should never sit at a full charge above 14.4V for extended periods unless it is an Absorbed Glass Mat (AGM) or Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4) system configured for higher voltages. Leaving a flooded battery at 15.7V can cause electrolyte loss, gassing, and eventual grid corrosion inside the cells.

To troubleshoot this without replacing hardware immediately, verify the battery type and the charger's specific algorithm. Many smart chargers allow you to adjust the absorption voltage via DIP switches or a small menu system. If your unit lacks digital controls, check the manual for the default voltage per cell (typically 2.35V per cell, totaling 14.1V for a 6-cell pack). If the device is stuck in a "bulk" phase indefinitely, it may be interpreting the battery as deeply discharged.

```bash
# Example: Checking terminal voltage with a multimeter during charging
# Connect red probe to positive terminal, black to negative
$ cat /dev/ttyUSB0 > charging_log.log 
# Monitor real-time voltage output in your serial monitor or log file
```

You can also use the `smart` command on some Linux-based diagnostic tools (if available) to inspect battery management system logs:

```bash
smartctl -a /dev/sdaX # Note: This is for disk health; ensure you are checking the right device context if using embedded BMS
```

More practically, disconnect the charger and measure the resting voltage of the battery. If it sits below 12.4V after a few hours off-charge, the cells may be sulfated and unable to accept a full charge at standard rates. In that case, a lower amperage setting (e.g., 2A instead of 6A) might help the charger overcome the internal resistance gradually without triggering false voltage limits.

If the charger continues to output 15.7V regardless of battery health, the unit may have an internal fault causing it to ignore absorption thresholds. In such cases, replacing the unit is the only safe option to prevent thermal runaway or permanent damage to your marine or motorcycle batteries. Always prioritize safety and verify voltage readings against manufacturer specifications before assuming a device is "smart" enough to handle extreme conditions autonomously.
